hero.summary: Tesamorelin is a synthetic 44-amino-acid analogue of human growth hormone-releasing factor, carrying a trans-3-hexenoyl group on the N-terminal tyrosine and an amide at the C-terminus. That single modification is what separates it from native GRF(1-44), and it is the reason the molecule survives long enough in circulation to be studied. Veracue supplies it as research material for laboratory work. It is not a medicine, and it is not the approved prescription product that shares its name.

quick_answer.heading: What tesamorelin actually is
quick_answer.body:
Tesamorelin, development code TH9507, is a growth hormone-releasing factor analogue. It binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells and prompts the pituitary to release its own growth hormone. Growth hormone then drives hepatic IGF-1 production. The molecule does not supply growth hormone directly, which is the main thing that separates it from recombinant GH.

The human evidence behind tesamorelin is unusually strong for a research peptide. It is also unusually narrow. Every pivotal trial studied adults living with HIV who had excess abdominal fat, using a specific pharmaceutical formulation. None of that evidence transfers automatically to a research-grade powder, to a different population, or to general weight loss. The approved label says so in plain terms.

chemical_identity.heading: Chemical identity and how to check it
chemical_identity.body:
Two CAS numbers circulate for this molecule, and confusing them is the most common identity error on vendor pages. The free peptide is CAS 218949-48-5. The acetate salt is CAS 901758-09-6, which is also the form used in the approved prescription product. Both describe the same 44-residue peptide. The difference is the counterion sitting alongside it, not the sequence.

PubChem CID 16137828 is the reference entry for the free base, with molecular formula C221H366N72O67S and an average molecular weight of 5135.9 g/mol. A laboratory receiving material can cross-check that record on arrival.
chemical_identity.mass_convention_note: Pages that print several different molecular weights without explaining them cause avoidable confusion. The 5135.9 figure is an average mass, calculated across natural isotope abundance. A mass spectrometry report usually matches a monoisotopic or exact mass instead, which is lower, because it uses the single most abundant isotope of each element. Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions, and a COA should state which convention its measured mass is compared against.

sequence.heading: The sequence, and the one part of it people get wrong
sequence.modification_notation: trans-3-hexenoyl-[GRF(1-44)]-NH2. The acyl group sits on the N-terminal tyrosine; the C-terminus is amidated.
sequence.body:
Tesamorelin keeps the complete native human GRF(1-44) backbone. Nothing inside the chain is substituted. The only non-native element is the trans-3-hexenoyl group attached at the N-terminus, which slows enzymatic breakdown and gives the molecule a circulating half-life of roughly 26 to 38 minutes rather than the couple of minutes native GHRH manages.

One correction worth making, because it appears on live vendor pages: position 2 is L-alanine, not D-alanine. The D-Ala2 substitution belongs to CJC-1295 and modified GRF(1-29). Copying it onto tesamorelin describes a different molecule. The FDA substance record gives the subunit as YADAIFTNSYRKVLGQLSARKLLQDIMSRQQGESNQERGARARL, and that is what an identity check should be run against.
sequence.presentation_note: Render the sequence in a monospaced block with the N-terminal modification labelled above it. The modification is part of the molecular identity, not a footnote.

salt_form.heading: Free base or acetate, and why it changes the number on the vial
salt_form.body:
Synthetic peptides are almost always isolated as a salt. For tesamorelin that salt is normally the acetate, with acetate counterions paired to the basic residues in the chain. The peptide sequence is identical either way. A counterion does not change which molecule you have.

What it does change is arithmetic. A vial filled by total mass contains peptide plus counterion plus residual water, so net peptide content is lower than the fill weight. How much lower depends on how many acetate counterions the lot carries and how much moisture it holds. That figure is lot-specific and belongs on the certificate, not in a general description.

Trifluoroacetate is the other counterion researchers encounter, usually left over from purification. TFA is heavier than acetate and carries its own handling considerations, so labs running cell-based work often specify acetate or a TFA-removal step. If the counterion matters to a protocol, it should be confirmed against the lot documentation rather than assumed from the product name.
salt_form.boundary_note: This section deliberately stops at analytical interpretation. No preparation arithmetic, no worked volumes, no concentration walkthrough. Adding those to a product page moves it toward administration guidance, which is outside research-use positioning.

mechanism.heading: How it works at the receptor
mechanism.chain: Tesamorelin → GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotrophs → endogenous growth hormone release → hepatic IGF-1 production → downstream GH effects including lipolysis
mechanism.body:
Tesamorelin binds the GHRH receptor, a class B G-protein-coupled receptor on the somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary. Receptor activation prompts those cells to release stored growth hormone in pulses, the way the pituitary normally does. Growth hormone then acts on the liver to raise IGF-1, which is the biomarker used throughout the clinical program to confirm the axis has been engaged.

That indirect route is the defining feature. Recombinant growth hormone delivers the hormone itself. Tesamorelin prompts the body to release its own, which is why trial reports describe restored pulsatile secretion rather than continuous exposure.

One thing the literature does not settle: why the fat loss lands so specifically on the visceral compartment. Several vendor pages explain it with a receptor-density argument presented as established fact. The editorial accompanying the 2019 Lancet HIV trial is more careful, noting that tesamorelin can stimulate lipolysis through increased endogenous growth hormone while multiple mechanisms may be at play. The selectivity is well documented in outcome data. The explanation for it is still open.

clinical_evidence.heading: What the human trials found, and in whom
clinical_evidence.body:
Tesamorelin sits apart from most compounds in a research catalog because it carries genuine randomized human evidence rather than cell and animal work alone. Being precise about that evidence matters more than amplifying it.

The pivotal study randomized 412 adults living with HIV who had accumulated abdominal fat, assigning 275 to tesamorelin and 137 to placebo for 26 weeks. Visceral adipose tissue fell 15.2 percent in the treatment arm while rising 5.0 percent on placebo. A pooled analysis of the two Phase 3 trials followed in 2010, with safety extension data.

Liver fat came later. A 12-month randomized trial in 61 participants with HIV and hepatic steatosis reported a 4.1 percentage-point absolute reduction in hepatic fat fraction against placebo, a 37 percent relative reduction. After a year, 35 percent of the tesamorelin group had hepatic fat below 5 percent, compared with 4 percent on placebo.

A 2026 meta-analysis pooled five randomized trials. Visceral adipose tissue fell by a mean 27.71 cm², trunk fat by 1.18 kg, hepatic fat by 4.28 percentage points, waist circumference by 1.61 cm. Lean body mass rose 1.42 kg. Subcutaneous fat and BMI did not change significantly, and neither did CD4+ counts. A separate 2026 systematic review reported a mean visceral reduction of 21.47 cm² with the same pattern of central selectivity.

analytical.heading: What the testing actually proves
analytical.intro: Purity claims do most of the persuading in this market and explain the least. Two methods appear on nearly every peptide COA, and they answer different questions. Reading them as interchangeable is where researchers get caught out.

rows.establishes: Chromatographic purity as percentage peak area. Separates the target peak from related peptides, truncated sequences and process impurities.
rows.does_not: Identity. A peak at the expected retention time is consistent with the target compound, not proof of it. Co-eluting species and compounds with weak UV absorbance can be missed.

rows.establishes: Molecular identity, by comparing measured mass against theoretical mass. Detects many sequence variants and modifications.
rows.does_not: A full impurity quantification. Species that ionize poorly may be underrepresented. A mass match also does not distinguish every isomeric possibility.

rows.method: Net peptide content (e.g. amino acid analysis)
rows.establishes: How much of the vial mass is actually peptide, separate from counterion and residual water.
rows.does_not: Sequence correctness or the presence of modifications.

rows.establishes: Which counterion is present and in what proportion.
Bacterial endotoxin load, which matters for cell-based work.
rows.does_not: Anything about identity, purity or potency.

analytical.orthogonality_note: Run together, chromatography and mass spectrometry cover each other's blind spots. That combination is why a figure like 99 percent by HPLC should be read as one measurement among several rather than a summary verdict on quality. It does not speak to sterility, endotoxin, counterion, net peptide content or biological activity.

veracue_program.heading: How Veracue documents a lot
veracue_program.body: Veracue publishes a four-stage process on its certificate archive: solid-phase synthesis in ISO-7 conditions, reverse-phase HPLC with peak area normalization at 214 nm against a ≥99.0 percent threshold, mass spectrometry for identity, and lyophilization under nitrogen backfill. Batch certificates from independent US laboratories are published in the archive and can be requested for a specific lot.
veracue_program.mandatory_disclosure: No Tesamorelin certificate currently sits in that archive. Until a lot is synthesized, tested and documented, this page must not state a purity figure, name a testing laboratory, or promise a COA for this compound. Veracue's own site disclaimer also notes purity varies by product and lot, and that some items may test below 99 percent.
veracue_program.publishing_instruction: When a Tesamorelin lot COA is issued, replace this block with the lot number, test date, laboratory name, measured purity, and the mass convention used for the identity match. Do not populate any of those fields from another compound's certificate.

regulatory.heading: The approved product is not this product
regulatory.body:
Tesamorelin is the active ingredient in an FDA-approved prescription product, and that fact gets misused constantly. Keeping the two apart is the single most important boundary on this page.

EGRIFTA WR (tesamorelin) for injection, manufactured by Theratechnologies, is approved for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adult patients with lipodystrophy. Initial U.S. approval was 2010, and the current label was revised in March 2025. The label states plainly that the product is not indicated for weight loss management, that long-term cardiovascular safety has not been established, and that EGRIFTA WR and EGRIFTA SV are not substitutable for one another.

Approval attaches to that specific product, from that manufacturer, made and released under pharmaceutical controls, for that population. It does not travel with the molecule. Research-grade tesamorelin is not an approved drug, is not interchangeable with any EGRIFTA formulation, and carries no pharmaceutical approval of any kind. Veracue is not the manufacturer of any approved tesamorelin product.

Nothing on this page is medical advice, and no statement here should be read as a therapeutic claim. faq.a: Tesamorelin is a synthetic 44-amino-acid analogue of human growth hormone-releasing factor. It carries a trans-3-hexenoyl group on its N-terminal tyrosine and an amide at the C-terminus, which slow enzymatic breakdown. It acts at the GHRH receptor on pituitary cells. Veracue supplies it as research material only.
TH9507 is the development code for tesamorelin, used in early trial reports and regulatory documents. It refers to the same molecule, not a different compound or a variant.

In one-letter code: YADAIFTNSYRKVLGQLSARKLLQDIMSRQQGESNQERGARARL-NH2, with a trans-3-hexenoyl group on the N-terminal tyrosine. It is the complete native human GRF(1-44) backbone with no internal substitutions. Position 2 is L-alanine. Sources showing D-alanine at position 2 are describing CJC-1295 or modified GRF(1-29), not tesamorelin.

faq.q: What is the molecular weight of tesamorelin?
faq.a: The average molecular weight of the free base is 5135.9 g/mol, with molecular formula C221H366N72O67S. A mass spectrometry report may compare against a monoisotopic or exact mass instead, which is a lower figure. Both are legitimate; a certificate should state which convention it used.

faq.q: What is the CAS number for tesamorelin?
faq.a: The free peptide is CAS 218949-48-5. The acetate salt is CAS 901758-09-6. Both refer to the same peptide sequence. Some vendor pages circulate other numbers for the acetate form that do not resolve to an authoritative record.

faq.q: Is tesamorelin acetate different from tesamorelin?
faq.a: The peptide is identical. Acetate is a counterion paired with the peptide during isolation. It affects solubility, handling and how much of the vial mass is actually peptide. It does not change the sequence or which molecule you have.

It binds the GHRH receptor on somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary, prompting release of the body's own growth hormone in pulses. Growth hormone then raises hepatic IGF-1. Tesamorelin does not supply growth hormone directly, which distinguishes it from recombinant GH.

faq.q: What receptor does tesamorelin act on?
faq.a: The GHRH receptor (GHRHR), a class B G-protein-coupled receptor on pituitary somatotrophs. This is worth separating from ghrelin-receptor agonists such as ipamorelin, which reach growth hormone release through a different receptor entirely.

faq.q: What does the clinical research show?
faq.a: In adults living with HIV and excess abdominal fat, a 412-participant randomized trial found visceral adipose tissue fell 15.2 percent over 26 weeks against a 5.0 percent rise on placebo. A 12-month trial in 61 participants found hepatic fat fraction fell 4.1 percentage points against placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis of five randomized trials found a mean visceral reduction of 27.71 cm² with no significant change in subcutaneous fat or BMI. All of this evidence comes from one clinical population using a pharmaceutical formulation.

faq.q: Does tesamorelin cause general weight loss?
faq.a: The randomized evidence does not support that. Pooled trials found no significant change in BMI or subcutaneous fat, and the approved prescription label states the product is not indicated for weight loss management because the effect is weight neutral. The documented change is compartment-specific, not a reduction in total body mass.

faq.q: What does a tesamorelin COA show?
faq.a: A useful certificate identifies the lot, the test date, the testing laboratory, the analytical methods, chromatographic purity by HPLC, and an identity result comparing measured mass against theoretical mass. Stronger certificates also report net peptide content and counterion. A certificate that reports only a purity percentage leaves most of the quality question unanswered.

faq.q: Does a 99 percent HPLC result mean the material is 99 percent pure in every sense?
faq.a: No. HPLC reports chromatographic purity as percentage peak area under one set of conditions. It does not confirm identity, quantify species that absorb weakly in UV, or account for counterion and residual water in the vial mass. Pairing it with mass spectrometry and a net peptide content figure gives a far more complete picture.

faq.q: Is tesamorelin FDA approved, and does that apply to this material?
faq.a: Tesamorelin is the active ingredient in EGRIFTA WR, approved for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adult patients with lipodystrophy. That approval belongs to that specific prescription product from its manufacturer. Research-grade tesamorelin is not an approved drug, is not interchangeable with any EGRIFTA formulation, and carries no pharmaceutical approval. Veracue does not manufacture any approved tesamorelin product.

Recommend omitting here. Worth a separate review of whether that tool should be linked from any compound page with an approved human analogue.

quality_gate.search_intent: Single job: identify and evaluate tesamorelin research material. No drift into treatment content.
quality_gate.information_gain: Five things competitors get wrong or skip, all corrected here: the acetate CAS, the D-Ala2 sequence error, the mass-convention confusion, the unsupported receptor-density explanation for visceral selectivity, and the absence of any subcutaneous fat or BMI effect.
quality_gate.aeo: Every FAQ and every section opens with a direct answer before explanation.
quality_gate.geo: Entity chain stated explicitly and defensibly: Tesamorelin → TH9507 → GHRF analogue → GHRH receptor → growth hormone → IGF-1 → visceral adipose tissue → HIV-associated lipodystrophy → analytical verification.
quality_gate.regulatory: Approved prescription product separated from research material in a dedicated section with a claim-classification table. No label dosing reproduced.
quality_gate.ruo: No dosing, no reconstitution arithmetic, no protocols, no human outcome framing. Calculator link deliberately withheld.
quality_gate.unresolved: The page cannot go live until a Tesamorelin product record and lot COA exist. Everything else is publish-ready.
